<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|breech|674|breeding}}</noinclude>'''3.''' To whip on the breech.
{{smaller block|Had not a courteous serving-man conveyed me away, whilst he went to fetch whips, I think, in my conscience, he would have ''breeched'' me.
{{right|''Robert Taylor'' (1612), Hog hath Lost his Pearl, vi.}}}}
'''4.''' To fit or furnish with a breech: as, to ''breech'' a gun.—'''5.''' To fasten by a breeching.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To suffer whipping on the breech.
{{smaller block|I am no ''breeching'' scholar in the schools.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 1.}}}}

¶'''breech-band''' (brēch′band), ''n.'' Same as ''breeching'', 3.

'''breech-barrow''' (brēch′bar″ō), ''n.'' A large high truck used in moving bricks in a brick-yard.

'''breech-block''' (brēch′blok), ''n.'' A movable piece at the breech of a breech-loading gun, which is withdrawn for the insertion of a cartridge and closed before firing, to receive the impact of the recoil.   ''E. H. Knight.'' See cut under ''breech-loader''.

'''breech-clout''' (brēch′klout), ''n.'' The cloth covering the breech, worn by American Indians and other uncivilized peoples.

'''breeches''' (brich′ez, formerly and still occasionally brē′chez), ''n. pl.''   [< ME. ''breche'', ''breches'', pl., usually ''breche'', ''brech'', also ''breke'', ''brek'' (> Sc. ''breeks'', ''breik'', etc.): see ''breech'', itself pl.]   '''1.''' A bifurcated garment worn by men, covering the body from the waist to the knees, or, in some cases, only to mid-thigh.—'''2.''' Less properly, trousers or pantaloons.{{smaller|—'''Breeches Bible.''' See ''Bible.''—'''To wear the breeches''', to usurp the authority of the husband: said of a wife.}}
{{smaller block|Children rule, old men go to school, women ''wear the breeches.''
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., To the Reader.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' See ''trousers''.}}

'''breeches-buoy''' (brich′ez-boi), ''n.'' In the life-saving service, a name given to an apparatus, like a short pair of breeches, moving on a rope {{img float|file=century v01 p0700 c1f1.png|width=161px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Breeches-buoy.}}}} stretched from a wreck to the shore, for the purpose of landing persons from the wreck.

'''breeching''' (brich′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''breech'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A whipping on the breech.
{{smaller block|I view the prince with Aristarchus’ eyes,
Whose looks were as a ''breeching'' to a boy.
{{right|''Marlowe'' (''and Shakspere''?), [Edw. III.}}}}
'''2.''' Hard, clotted wool on the buttocks of a sheep.—'''3.''' That part of a horse’s harness which passes round its breech, and which enables it to back the vehicle to which it is harnessed. The breeching is connected by straps to the saddle and shafts. Also called ''breech-band''. See cut under ''harness''.—'''4.''' In ''naval gun.'', a strong rope passed through a hole in the cascabel of a gun and fastened to bolts in the ship’s side, to check the recoil of the gun when it is fired.—'''5.''' A bifurcated smoke-pipe of a furnace.

'''breeching-bolt''' (brich′ing-bōlt), ''n.'' A bolt in a ship’s side to which the breeching is fastened.

'''breeching-hook''' (brich′ing-hu̇k), ''n.'' A curved hook on the shafts of a carriage to which the breeching of the harness is secured.

'''breeching-loop''' (brich′ing-löp), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a loop of metal formerly cast on the breech of guns, through which the breeching was passed.

'''breechless''' (brēch′les), ''a.'' Without breeches; hence, naked.
{{smaller block|He bekez by the bale fyre, and ''breklesse'' hyme semede.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1048.}}}}

'''breech-loader''' (brēch′lō″dėr), ''n.'' A firearm loaded at the breech. {{smaller|The term is generally confined to small arms, whether used in hunting or in war, large guns being usually referred to as ''breech-loading cannon.''}}

[[File:century v01 p0700 c1f2.png|center|289px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Springfield Breech-loader.}}}}
{{c|{{smaller|Side-view of gun with breech-block, ''d'', thrown up; ''c'', breech-pin; ''h'', firing-pin; ''m'', thumb-piece.}}}}

{{smaller|The earliest European firearms were made to load at the breech; but as soon as accuracy of aim and long range were demanded this plan was abandoned, as the mechanical appliances of the day did not allow of accurate fitting and quick working of the breech-piece. Since about 1840, however, breech-loading firearms have been made success-}}
{{smaller|fully, and have gradually come into general use for all purposes. Rapidity of firing, ease of cleaning, and close adjustment of the missile to the bore, excluding windage, are the advantages of this form of arm.}}

[[File:century v01 p0700 c2f1.png|center|344px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Martini Breech-loader.}}}}

'''breech-loading''' (brēch′lō″ding), ''a.'' Receiving the charge at the breech instead of the muzzle: applied to firearms: as, a ''breech-loading'' rifle.

'''breech-mechanism''' (brēch′mek″a̤-nizm), ''n.'' The parts comprised in the breech of a gun; specifically, the mechanical device for opening and closing the breech of a gun in loading and firing.

'''breech-piece''' (brēch′pēs), ''n.'' '''1.''' The wrought-iron welded coil shrunk on the rear end of the steel tubes of the Fraser system of heavy guns.
{{smaller block|Over the rear end of the steel tube is shrunk a very powerful coil, called the ''breech-piece.''
{{right|''Ure'', Dict., IV. 83.}}}} '''2.''' A heavy mass of steel which supports the wedge in the Krupp system of guns.

'''breech-pin''' (brēch′pin), ''n.'' In ''gun.'', a mounted plug screwed into the rear end of the barrel of a firearm. {{smaller|In a breech-loader the plug forms the bottom of the charging-chamber or well; in a muzzle-loader it forms the bottom of the bore.}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0700 c2f2.png|width=222px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Breech-pin. ''a'', plug; ''b'', tenon; ''c'', tang; ''d'', tang-screw hole; ''e'', face.}}}}

'''breech-screw''' (brēch′skrö), ''n.'' Same as ''breech-pin.''

'''breech-sight''' (brēch′sīt), ''n.'' That sight of a gun which is placed next the breech; the hind sight.

'''breech-wrench''' (brēch′rench), ''n.'' A wrench employed in turning out the breech-pin of a muzzle-loading firearm.

'''breed''' (brēd), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bred'', ppr. ''breeding.''   [< ME. ''breden'', < AS. ''brēdan'', nourish, cherish, keep warm (= D. ''broeden'' = MLG. ''broden'', LG. ''brȫden'' = OHG. ''bruoten'', MHG. ''brüeten'', G. ''brüten'', brood, hatch), < ''brōd'', brood: see ''brood'', ''n.'', and cf. ''brood'', ''v.'' ''Breed'' is related to ''brood'' as ''feed'' to ''food.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To procreate; beget; engender; hatch.
{{smaller block|Yet every mother ''breeds'' not sons alike.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 3.}}}}
'''2†.''' To produce within or upon the body by development or organic process.
{{smaller block|The worms . . . that did ''breed'' the silk. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Children would ''breed'' their teeth with less danger.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
'''3.''' To cause; occasion; produce; originate.
{{smaller block|<poem>What pains
I have bestow’d, to ''breed'' this present peace.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I honour philosophicall instructions, and blesse the wits which ''bred'' them.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>E’en when sober truth prevails throughout,
They swear it, till affirmance ''breeds'' a doubt.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Conversation.}}}}
{{smaller block|Intemperance and lust ''breed'' infirmities.
{{right|''Tillotson.''}}}}
'''4.''' To produce; be the native place of: as, a pond ''breeds'' fish; a northern country ''breeds'' a race of stout men.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hail, foreign wonder!
Whom certain these rough shades did never ''breed.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 266.}}}}
{{smaller block|Why doth Africa ''breed'' so many venomous beasts, Ireland none?
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 293.}}}}
{{smaller block|The barren soil does not ''breed'' fevers, crocodiles, tigers, or scorpions.
{{right|''Emerson'', Compensation.}}}}
'''5.''' To bring up; nurse and foster; take care of during the period of growth: as, born and ''bred.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Young Archas,
A boy as sweet as young; my brother ''breeds'' him,
My noble brother Brisky ''breeds'' him nobly.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, v. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ah! wretched me! by fates averse decreed
To bring thee forth with pain, with care to ''breed.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
{{smaller block|To ''breed up'' the son to common sense.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires.}}}}
{{smaller block|The trade he ''breeds'' them ''up'' in.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
'''7.''' To procure by the mating of parents, and rear for use: as, to ''breed'' canaries; to ''breed'' cattle for the market.—{{smaller|'''Bred out,''' degenerated.}}
{{smaller block|The strain of man’s ''bred out''
Into baboon and monkey.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Well bred,''' having good manners; well instructed: as, his actions show him to be ''well bred.'' See ''well-bred.''}}
{{smaller block|A gentleman ''well bred'', and of good name.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|I have not seen a cobbler [in Paris] who is not ''better bred'' than an English gentleman.
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', To Mrs. Sydney Smith.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' To generate.—'''5.''' To nourish, nurture.—'''6.''' To educate, school, discipline.—'''7.''' To raise.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To beget or bear offspring; produce young; be fruitful: used figuratively of increase generally.
{{smaller block|That they may ''breed'' abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful.
{{right|Gen. viii. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|Where they most ''breed'' and haunt.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|I make it [money] ''breed'' as fast.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The mother had never ''bred'' before.
{{right|''Carpenter.''}}}}
'''2.''' To have birth; be produced; arise; grow; develop: as, maggots ''breed'' readily in carrion.
{{smaller block|<poem>As fester’d members rot but by degree,
Till bones, and flesh, and sinews fall away,
So will this base and envious discord ''breed.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iii. 1.}}}} '''3.''' To procure the birth of young: with ''from'': as, to ''breed from'' a mare of good stock.—'''4†.''' To be pregnant.
{{smaller block|Mercy, being a young and ''breeding'' woman, longed for something that she saw there, but was ashamed to ask.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii., Shepherds.}}}}

{{smaller block|'''To breed in and in''', to breed from animals of the same stock that are closely related.—'''To breed true''', to produce offspring exhibiting the same characteristics of form, color, and general qualities as the parents: said of animals, poultry, etc., of pure breed.}}

'''breed''' (brēd), ''n.''   [< ''breed'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A race or progeny from the same parents or stock; especially, a race of men or other animals having an alliance by nativity and some distinctive qualities in common, which are transmitted by heredity; hence, family; extraction: as, a ''breed'' of men in a particular country; horses or sheep of good ''breed''.
{{smaller block|<poem>I bring you witnesses,
Twice fifteen thousand hearts of England’s ''breed''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The farmer race of Arabs, the most despised by their fellow countrymen, and the most hard-favored, morally as well as physically, of all the ''breed''.
{{right|''R. F. Burton'', El-Medinah, p. 250.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' Sort; kind: in a general sense.
{{smaller block|This courtesy is not of the right ''breed''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2.}}}}
'''3†.''' A number produced at once; a hatch; a brood: as, “above an hundred at a ''breed'',” ''N. Grew''.—'''4†.''' Increase of any sort, especially interest on money; usury.
{{smaller block|<poem>For when did friendship take
A ''breed'' of barren metal of his friend?</poem> {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3.}}}}
'''5†.''' Breeding.
{{smaller block|That countrey is a very greate soyle of cattell, and verye fitt for ''breede''. {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}

'''breed-bate†''' (brēd′bāt), ''n.''   [< ''breed'', ''v.'', + obj. ''bate''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.'']   One who breeds or incites to quarrels: as, “no tell-tale nor no ''breed-bate'',” ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 4.

'''breeder''' (brē′dėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who or that which breeds, procreates, or produces young: used especially of the female.
{{smaller block|You love the ''breeder'' better than the male.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' One who educates or rears; figuratively, that which rears.
{{smaller block|Italy and Rome have been the best ''breeders'' . . . of the worthiest men. {{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster.}}}}
'''3.''' One who or that which produces, causes, or brings about: as, he was a ''breeder'' of dissensions.
{{smaller block|Time is the nurse and ''breeder'' of all good.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' One who procures the birth of young; one who raises a particular breed, as of animals; technically, in herd- and stud-books, the owner of the dam at the time of the birth of the animal recorded.—'''5†.''' Same as ''bred-sore''.

'''breeding''' (brē′ding), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''breed'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of generating or producing.—'''2.''' The rearing of cattle or live stock of any kind, particularly by mingling or crossing one strain<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
